newsitem.title: UK: UK economy faces building society windfall dilemma.
newsitem.headline: UK economy faces building society windfall dilemma.

text.p: The British economy will get the answer to a make-or-break question this summer -- how much of a flood of windfall payments from building societies will be spent rather than saved.

With building societies rushing headlong to convert into banks and forking out about 20 billion sterling in one-off share payments to customers in the process, that answer could dictate whether the domestic economy spirals wildly out of control.
The government, in line with classical economic theory, assumes the lion's share will be saved. But what if it is wrong?

"We assume 25 percent of the windfalls will be spent this year, adding about one percent to consumer spending," said Michael Saunders, UK economist at Salomon Brothers. That would foster buoyant growth but no boom, he added.
On Monday, the Halifax, Britain's largest mortgage lender, got overwhelming approval fom its members to float on the stock exchange. It will be valued at about 12 billion sterling.

Following hot on the heels of the Halifax, the Woolwich, Alliance & Leicester and Northern Rock Building Societies will all shed their mutual status, while the Bristol & West Building Society will be bought by Bank of Ireland. Members are unlikely to look those gift horses in the mouth either.

U.S. investment bank Salomon Brothers has commissioned a survey on the windfalls from pollsters MORI. It showed roughly one-third of the adult population will receive a windfall and most people expect to get a bit more than 1,000 pounds.
The worst-case scenario for UK Plc -- that the whole lot is spent -- would be equivalent to a one-off income tax cut of about 10 pence in the pound, but nobody expects that.

Nonetheless, if just five billion sterling is spent it would dwarf the effect of the one penny sliced off the basic rate of income tax Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke unveiled at last November's budget.
That was equivalent to pumping about two billion sterling into the economy. And some economists thought even that was excessive given healthy levels of high street spending.
The government, which is already forecasting consumer spending growth of 4.25 percent this year, said last week it expected the bulk of windfall payments to be saved.

"The Treasury has assumed that most of this money will not be spent, at least in the short term," the government said in a response to Treasury Select Committee questions. "Hence the effects on consumer spending and GDP are expected to be relatively small."

But some economists are not so sure. "The building society bonuses will reinforce the spending power of consumers who seem already willing to take on debt to finance their expenditures," said Stephen Lewis, chief economist at London Bond Broking.

He agreed that economic theory suggests windfalls are saved but said this time could be very different. "So substantial are the sums concerned the chances are that personal spending will diverge from the textbook norm and that the boost to expenditure could be considerably larger (than 25 percent spent)."
Saunders said the fact that a large amount of the cash will go to middle-aged, upper income groups steeped in the savings culture, meant a dangerous spending spree would be avoided.

And given that a high proportion of the spending will go on holidays -- money largely spend abroad -- the pressure on domestic inflation may be muted, although Britain's trade position may deteriorate, he said.

Lewis was less sure. While some investors -- so-called carpetbaggers -- may have deposited funds with building societies solely to grab windfall payments and will have smoothed out their spending in anticipation, he said they will be firmly in the minority.

"Most building society savers and borrowers have probably formed no clear idea of the largesse that is about to descend on them," he said. "The conclusion is that consumer spending, already growing at four percent annually, is more likely to accelerate than to subside."
